2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). raw_response.chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable / Unclear (cross-sectional single-year 2004 national dataset with no longitudinal follow-up; however, item-level missingness across the 101 countries required Amelia II multivariate imputation and forced exclusion of the Gini inequality indicator, with exact missingness rates not reported in this paper).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High risk (single-year cross-sectional ecological design at national scale; 25 indicators are collapsed into 5 PCA composite pillars discretized into 2-3 levels, bundling governance effectiveness [WGI GE] inside the Human Development and Poverty [HDP] composite alongside GDP per capita, poverty, slums, health, and schooling so governance cannot be separated from economic development; income inequality [Gini] was omitted due to missingness; bidirectional/reverse causality is acknowledged).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak / High concern (legal and institutional governance constructs are proxied only by economy-wide perception-based Worldwide Governance Indicators [WGI GE, which bundles rule of law, regulatory quality, and control of corruption; WGI PS AV; WGI VA] and counts/indices of international environmental treaty participation [Particip], discretized into 2 or 3 coarse k-means bins, with zero water- or sanitation-sector-specific statutory, regulatory, or municipal enforcement measurement).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High risk (authors explicitly warn that the compiled secondary dataset has strong heterogeneity of sources and collection methods and should not be used for quantitative interpretation; continuous indicators are discretized into 2 or 3 k-means classes causing information loss; WGI measures rely on subjective expert assessments).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate-to-high concern (national water supply [WS] and sanitation [S] coverage come from the standardized 2004 WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme [JMP] benchmark, but rely on heterogeneous underlying national surveys, omit drinking water quality and service reliability, and are dichotomized via k-means into just two broad categories: WS 22-82% vs >82-100%, and S 9-58% vs >58-100%).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Some concern / No pre-analysis plan (no pre-registered protocol; variable reduction from 42 to 25 indicators was data-driven based on preliminary correlations/collinearity in Dondeynaz et al. 2012, DAG edge directions combine PCA with subjective author judgement, and detailed country-profile scenario reporting focuses selectively on Profiles 4 and 5, though error rates and sensitivity metrics are reported across models).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate concern (sample covers 101 developing countries in 2004 while excluding developed countries, small states, and islands, but exact operational cut-offs for exclusion criteria, the full country roster, and item-level missingness proportions prior to Amelia II imputation are deferred to a companion paper rather than reported in full).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper states that the sample comprises 101 developing countries in 2004 and excludes developed countries, small states, and islands, and notes that variable inclusion (25 of 42 indicators) was based on correlation and collinearity screening. However, the operational thresholds defining 'developing countries', 'small states', and 'islands' are deferred to Dondeynaz et al. (2012) rather than fully specified within this article.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
domain_ratings.justification: The national scale, reference year (2004), variable ranges and discretization cut-offs (Table A1), and sample sizes across the five country profiles (Table 7, summing to N = 101, with partial country examples for Profiles 3, 4, and 5) are reported, but the complete list of 101 countries and country-level missing-data rates are not presented in this paper (referred instead to Dondeynaz et al., 2012).
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.1 (PDF Pages 2-3); Section 4.3, Table 7 (PDF Pages 14-16); Table A1 (PDF Page 19)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Exposures (governance, human development, environmental commitment, agricultural water pressure, and ODA) are compiled from heterogeneous secondary country-level sources that the authors explicitly warn should not be used for quantitative interpretation. Governance exposures rely on economy-wide subjective expert perceptions (WGI) rather than water/sanitation legal or institutional measures, missing data are imputed via Amelia II without reporting missingness proportions, and exposures are collapsed into PCA first components and discretized into 2 or 3 k-means bins.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.1-2.2 (PDF Pages 2-3); Section 3.2 (PDF Pages 4-5); Section 5 (PDF Pages 17-18); Table A1 (PDF Page 19)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
domain_ratings.justification: International agencies (WHO/UNICEF JMP, World Bank, FAO, OECD) supply standardized indicator definitions at macro level, but country condition classifications (the five country profiles and LOW/MID/HIGH variable states) are constructed via sample-dependent PCA and k-means clustering rather than external objective thresholds, and underlying country data collection methods are heterogeneous.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.1-2.2 (PDF Pages 2-3); Section 3.2 (PDF Pages 4-5); Section 4.3 (PDF Page 14); Table A1 (PDF Page 19)

domain_ratings.justification: The authors explicitly identify key macro-level socio-economic, demographic, environmental, and financial confounders (GDP per capita, poverty headcount, urban population, slum share, child mortality, malaria, schooling, water resource availability, agricultural withdrawals, and ODA) as well as unmeasured confounders including income inequality (Gini index), drinking water quality, and cultural/psychological sanitation norms.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.1, Figure 1 (PDF Pages 2-3); Section 4.1.1 (PDF Pages 6-7); Section 5 (PDF Page 18)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domain_ratings.justification: No rigorous strategy isolates specific institutional or policy exposures from macro-level confounders. Aggregating 25 variables into 5 coarse PCA pillars and discretizing them into 2-3 bins induces severe residual confounding—most notably bundling governance effectiveness (WGI GE, proxying rule of law, regulatory quality, and corruption control) inside the HDP pillar alongside GDP per capita and poverty in a naive Bayes structure where HDP is the parent node. Income inequality (Gini) was dropped due to missing data, and cross-sectional simultaneity ('chicken-egg situation') is unaddressed.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.2 (PDF Page 5); Section 4.1.1 (PDF Pages 6-7); Section 4.2-4.2.1, Figure 4 (PDF Pages 9-11)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Water supply (WS) and sanitation (S) coverage come from the 2004 WHO/UNICEF JMP global monitoring dataset, an established international benchmark, but suffer from cross-country survey heterogeneity, omit water quality and service continuity, and are coarsely dichotomized via k-means into just two broad intervals (WS: 22-82% vs >82-100%; S: 9-58% vs >58-100%), which the authors acknowledge causes information loss and increases classification error.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.1-2.2 (PDF Pages 2-3); Section 3.2 (PDF Pages 4-5); Section 5 (PDF Page 18); Table A1 (PDF Page 19)

domain_ratings.justification: While Bayesian networks can represent conditional dependencies, the analytical pipeline incurs major distortion by collapsing subvariables into first-PCA components, discretizing continuous outcomes into 2 k-means bins, failing to propagate Amelia II multiple-imputation uncertainty, evaluating classification error rates purely in-sample (producing apparent 0% error rates in small N = 17-24 country-profile subsamples due to overfitting), and interpreting cross-sectional ecological conditional probabilities as directional policy targets.
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract (PDF Page 1); Section 2.2 (PDF Page 3); Section 3.2 (PDF Pages 4-5); Section 4.1-4.3, Tables 1 & 7 (PDF Pages 5-15)

evidence_quotes.criterion: Q1 & Q2 — Sample inclusion criteria and national cross-sectional target group
evidence_quotes.quote: The observations include 101 developing countries (our target group), therefore developed countries but also small states and islands are excluded.

evidence_quotes.criterion: Q3 & Q7 — Data source heterogeneity and explicit warning against quantitative interpretation
evidence_quotes.quote: The WatSan4Dev data set should be considered for qualitative analysis and not for quantitative interpretation purposes because of the strong heterogeneity of the sources and the data collection methods

evidence_quotes.criterion: Q5 & Q6 — Omitted confounder (income inequality / Gini index excluded due to missing data)
evidence_quotes.quote: The indicator of inequality could not be integrated into these models. Indeed, the Gini index that measures the inequality of income at country level showed too many missing values

evidence_quotes.criterion: Q6 & Q8 — Naive Bayes pillar aggregation mediating links between WSS and subvariables such as governance
evidence_quotes.quote: An indirect link is created from WSS variables to subvariables with the CI as intermediate variable.

evidence_quotes.criterion: Q3 & Legal measurement quality — Absence of subsector-disaggregated governance and corruption data
evidence_quotes.quote: Having such breakdowns or at least, compared case studies on corruption mechanisms in both subsectors could help in providing more accurate interpretations.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: High methodological concern under the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies. S181 models single-year (2004) cross-national observational data for 101 developing countries from the WatSan4Dev database using discrete Bayesian networks and simple bivariate linear regression. Although the study transparently discusses data limitations and identifies broad macro-level correlates of water supply and sanitation (WSS) coverage, it has substantial internal-validity weaknesses for empirical policy or legal-institutional inference: (1) all variables derive from heterogeneous secondary macro-indicators that the authors themselves caution are unsuitable for quantitative interpretation, with unreported item-level missingness imputed via Amelia II prior to modelling; (2) legal and governance constructs are measured only via economy-wide subjective perception aggregates (Worldwide Governance Indicators) and international treaty signatures rather than water/sanitation-specific legal or regulatory rules; (3) continuous exposures and JMP WSS outcomes are compressed into 5 PCA composite pillars and k-means discretized into 2 or 3 broad bins, bundling governance effectiveness (WGI GE) inside the Human Development and Poverty (HDP) composite so institutional effects cannot be disentangled from GDP per capita or poverty; and (4) model error rates are assessed purely in-sample (including small N = 17-24 country-profile subsets) while cross-sectional conditional probabilities are frequently framed as directional policy requirements despite ecological aggregation and acknowledged reverse causality.
raw_response.study_design_identified: Cross-national analytical cross-sectional observational study (Bayesian network probabilistic modelling and bivariate linear regression of 2004 country-level indicators across 101 developing countries)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Study design, 2004 cross-sectional WatSan4Dev sample (N = 101 developing countries), and pre-processing/imputation are in Section 1 and Sections 2.1-2.2 (PDF Pages 2-3). Bayesian network methodology, k-means discretization, PCA composite pillar construction, and naive Bayes submodel structures are in Sections 3.1-3.2 and 4.1-4.2 (PDF Pages 3-9), with discretization bounds in Table A1 (PDF Page 19). Model fit, scenario simulations, bivariate WS-S regression, and five country-profile submodels are in Sections 4.1-4.3 and Tables 1-9 and B1 (PDF Pages 5-17, 20). Governance (WGI) validity debates, missing sector disaggregation, and omitted water-quality/cultural variables are discussed in Section 5 (PDF Pages 17-18).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study analyses a single-year (2004) quantitative cross-section of 101 developing countries to estimate conditional probabilistic associations (explicitly framed as a non-parametric alternative to regression models, alongside an OLS linear regression) between socio-economic, environmental, governance, and aid indicators and national water/sanitation coverage. There is no policy/intervention comparator or quasi-experimental design (ruling out ROBINS-I), no longitudinal follow-up (ruling out JBI Cohort), and no primary qualitative empirical data collection (ruling out CASP and MMAT; the paper's 'qualitative dimension' refers solely to subjective Bayesian probability theory and discretizing quantitative national indicators into low/medium/high classes). Therefore, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact matching instrument.
